title: Saber CEO hides jab at Randy Pitchford in game trailer as payback for Pitchford dumping on Embracer: 'Without Embracer, Randy is performing magic tricks at birthday parties for a living'
summary: I love low-stakes drama.
body: If you watched the recent trailer for Saber Interactive's upcoming Rideshare 'Stimulator' (the quotation marks are part of the title) you may have thought it seemed a little bit hinky in spots. Midway through the video, after a quick rundown of some of the game's oddball passengers, the narrator says, "And when I think I've met the randiest of passengers, someone even stranger gets it." First of all, who says "randy"—a synonym, mostly British, for "horny"—anymore, aside from people in those cozy English countryside murder mystery TV shows my mom likes? And second, where are these randy people to begin with? Nobody in the video looks all that revved up to me. A few seconds later, another oddity: A personalized Texas license plate, not zoomed in enough to be conspicuous but clear enough to read without trouble: USB DRV. And there's sort of a gear-looking thing on it too, not the sort of symbol traditionally associated with the Lone Star State. (Image credit: Unigine) It's something I would never have picked up on, because I tend to not pay much attention to what's going on around me. Fortunately, Stephen Totilo at Game File did notice, and he asked Saber Interactive CEO Matt Kartch …

title: Mark Zuckerberg's rambling AI manifesto is 6,434 words of high-handed platitudes and dubious conclusions
summary: Tell us what you really think. No actually, don't.
body: I've spent a large part of my morning reading the words of Mark Zuckerberg. 6,434 of them, to be precise, if we're including the "Mark" signoff at the bottom. The Meta CEO (and everyone's favourite smart glasses advocate ) has written what can only be described as a manifesto regarding upcoming "superintelligent" AI technology—and I'll be honest, my eyes have glazed over more than once. The piece/blog post/rambling diatribe has been posted on Meta's website, under the title " The Future is for Everyone: The Path to a Positive AI Future ." If you'll allow me, I'd like to quote some choice insights: "The defining questions of our age are who will have access to superintelligence and what will we direct it towards. Will it be centralized and restricted to a few institutions, or will it be a tool that empowers everyone?" asks Zuckerberg. "We propose a philosophy based on individual empowerment as the source of prosperity, invention as the primary purpose of superintelligence, and balance of power as the foundation of safety." How will that work out, exactly? Well hold on for multiple paragraphs, because we'll get there eventually. Before that, though, Zuckerberg has some scene setting…

title: It's time to update Asus Armoury Crate and several other Asus software tools again, as another high severity security vulnerability has been discovered
summary: Sounds like a nasty one.
body: Asus Armoury Crate is not my favourite bit of software. It looks all high-tech on the surface, but any time I use it for more than five minutes, I'm reminded of the fact it's rather messy. It's also hit the headlines previously for patched security vulnerability issues—and good news, folks, here we go again. Per the Asus security advisory board , Armoury Crate, Asus GPU Tweak III, and GPU Tweak II should all be updated to ensure "optimal protection," after the discovery of a new security vulnerability. Listed as CVE-2026-8917 , the issue has been given a score of 8.4 out of 10, with a "high" severity rating. Which is, funnily enough, the exact same rating as the previous issue we wrote about last year. "An IOCTLY vulnerability allows a local attacker to write a specific value to an arbitrary memory address, potentially leading to privilege escalation," says the posting. Well, that sounds like something that should be patched up at the earliest possible moment. The CVE listing doesn't mention Armoury Crate specifically, but the Asus page mentions that "a component used" by the software is part of the update, so time to get installing. title: GTA 6 might not technically be $100, but it's had its cake and ate it too as pre-orders are 'skewing more to the premium edition'
summary: Schrodinger's price change.
body: Grand Theft Auto 6's potential price-point was a thing of much consternation in the lead-up to its reveal. Months of rumours —and even the Bank of America getting involved in the discourse, because why not—led to the question: Are they really gonna charge $100 for this thing? You're reading this article because they didn't, but you're also reading this article because they sort of did. See, GTA 6 has both an $80 version and a $100 version, the latter of which hides some potentially major parts of its identity behind the upgrade , including a handful of stores that may very well remind you that you've not shelled out every time you go near them. There's this itchy capitalist feeling that Rockstar probably did actually want to charge a hundo for the thing, but didn't, because that'd have gamers up in arms—as it turns out, that might've been the smart play. title: As if PCs weren't expensive enough already, Microsoft is reportedly now charging OEMs more for Windows licenses
summary: Supposedly, it's a "significant increase."
body: Taiwanese news site United Daily News reports that, according to one source, Microsoft is charging Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) significantly more for Windows licensing fees this year than in previous years (via Wccftech ). These are the fees that PC makers, for instance, must pay to Microsoft to package their machines with the operating system. UDN says (via machine translation): "A PC brand executive stated that Microsoft increases licensing fees for Windows OEMs every year. In the past, licensing fees mostly increased by single digits each year, but starting in July this year, the average increase has reached 7% to 10%, which is a significant increase compared to previous years." I can't confirm whether UDN's source is correct, but given Framework recently said it's seen an increase in Windows license costs , I have no reason to doubt it. Apparently Microsoft charges OEMs more for Windows licenses if they're used with higher-end CPUs—which seems like a strange decision to me given it shouldn't actually change anything about the operating system being delivered, but I'm not a business bigwig so what do I know? title: Firefox stunts on Edge as Microsoft gears up to neuter adblockers: 'uBlock Origin isn't going anywhere'
summary: Blocked. Blocked. Blocked. None of these corpo browsers are free of sin.
body: Earlier this year, Google Chrome annoyed a whole lot of adblock users by killing support for Manifest V2 extensions . It's a Manifest V3 world now, which means the permissions and APIs that thoroughgoing adblockers like uBlock Origin rely on are a thing of the past on Chrome (it's since been replaced by a pared-down version: uBlock Origin Lite ). Now, Microsoft Edge is following suit: "Over the next few months, MV2 extensions will be gradually turned off by default," says Redmond . All of which is red meat for the folks over at Mozilla Firefox, the free-and-open-source browser that once reigned supreme on our PCs before Chrome came and ate its lunch. In posts across social media, Firefox kicked Edge (and Chrome) in their self-inflicted bruises, declaring that "Our support for uBlock Origin isn't going anywhere", a post that came days after it wrote "Reminder that you can still just… use ad blockers on Firefox. Wild concept, we know." Now, like I said, it's not like Chromium-based browsers are murdering adblockers wholesale. title: id Software dev says mass layoffs like Microsoft's are weakening the games industry, because developers 'don't have the incentive to care anymore'
summary: "A lot of gamers, even if they don't know it, they can feel it's not right. There's something wrong."
body: At the end of last month, id Software lead services programmer Chris Hayes offered a blunt appraisal of Xbox's management during an interview with YouTube channel Auf ein Bier, saying Microsoft's repeated mass layoffs have proved that its leadership "fundamentally don't understand art." Elsewhere in the interview, Hayes expanded the scope of his criticism beyond the immediate damage wrought by the latest round of Xbox cuts . Looking at the industry more broadly, Hayes, who's still a Microsoft employee, says mass layoffs and nearsighted cost cutting are producing worse games, because they're denying game developers the opportunity—and motivation—to improve their craft. While major companies like Microsoft might brag about the "great IPs and studios" that they own, Hayes said they seem incapable of understanding that they regularly harm their own capability to produce anything of value with those brands and developers. "It is our experience together, our working together, and our past experiences that make the studio good. title: 'Thank you so much for the best weekend ever': The id Software gang got together at QuakeCon, and it sure looks like everyone had a great time
summary: I love a happy ending.
body: The recently concluded QuakeCon was a big one, marking the 30th anniversary of the game that started it all and, more notably, bringing id Software co-founders Adrian Carmack, John Carmack, Tom Hall, and John Romero together for the first time in a very long time. I had wondered, in the lead-up to the event, if it might get a little awkward or uncomfortable: Differences between the Johns were " over-dramatized " over the years, according to Romero Games co-founder Brenda Romero, but Adrian Carmack filed a lawsuit over his removal from the studio back in 2005, and other internal conflicts over the years led to the dismissal of well-liked employees like American McGee and Paul Steed. The more recent layoffs of Xbox that left the studio in varying states of " gutted ," depending on who you ask, also threatened to overshadow the whole thing. So, you know: you wonder . Now that everything is wrapped up, I'm happy to report that if there was any awkwardness or discomfort between the studio's famed founders, everyone kept it to themselves and they all seemed to have a really good time. "QuakeCon was fantastic this year, especially reuniting with the original founders!" John Carmack wrote…

title: Corsair isn't rolling in money from its mega-expensive RAM kits—and it's all thanks to higher component costs and lower demand
summary: The memory crisis is a complicated beast.
body: If you've looked at memory prices recently, you've probably seen Corsair DIMMs selling for astonishing prices. The 32 GB Vengeance DDR5 RGB kit sitting in my PC right now is selling for $480 at Amazon , whereas I bought it for $90-$100 just a couple of years ago. Corsair RAM can still be some of the cheapest comparatively , but it's very pricey nonetheless. So, Corsair must be raking in money hand over fist, right? Not quite, at least according to its recent filings with the SEC . The figures show a ~9% decline in Q2 2026 gaming component and system revenue overall compared to last year—although gross profit was up 17%. Memory revenue itself has increased, but its "other component products" revenue has decreased significantly. According to the company: "We are both a seller of memory products and a purchaser of memory and other components from third-party suppliers. As a result, elevated pricing benefits net sales and margin on the memory products we sell, while also increasing our cost of components across our broader product offerings." title: Dev at id Software says Microsoft 'burned a lot of bridges' in the industry: 'They fundamentally don't understand art, they don't understand games'
summary: "The way they align their spreadsheets for their financial reports—is not the way we used to do it."
body: One of the biggest tragedies of Xbox's wide-reaching reset is id Software, which was cut by a whopping 136 roles . And while official statements from Microsoft and the studio have tried to reassure players that it's not been gutted , whether that's just a panicking Xbox trying to calm anxieties is up for debate. Especially given the words of Chris Hays, lead services programmer at id Software, in an interview with YouTube channel Auf ein Bier at the end of last month. To say that Hays doesn't mince his words is an understatement—and I'm finding it hard to blame him, given Microsoft announced the layoffs one day before Doom: The Dark Ages released its DLC . " Everyone had just gotten off of a worse-than-usual crunch to get the DLC out the door, finally get a breather, and we were excited for our launch on the Tuesday … Instead of watching in anticipation for people, streamers, and seeing all the hard work they put in finally pay off? Now they don't know what they're doing." title: Valve has added 'initial' SteamOS gamepad support for several new gaming handhelds, including the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+
summary: Along with a host of bug fixes, of course.
body: Valve is still beavering away at the internals of SteamOS, and the latest update notes for the 3.8.25 Beta release mention the addition of "initial gamepad support" for several non-Valve gaming handhelds. The mighty MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ is on the list, as are two offerings from Ayaneo. These are the Ayaneo Pocket S2 , an Android-first, Snapdragon-powered device that launched in June of last year, and the Konkr Fit , a recently-launched Windows handheld released under one of Ayaeno's sub-brands. The Fit comes in two AMD APU flavours, the Ryzen AI 9 HX 470 and the Ryzen AI 9 HX 370. It's also got TMR joysticks and Hall effect triggers, which should hopefully benefit from the latest update. Tucked away at the bottom of the "Non-Valve Devices" section is a note on updated gamepad support for the OneXPlayer Apex . You know, the one with an optional plug-in liquid cooling tower released back in the pre-memory crisis times, when ultra-high-end handhelds made a small modicum of sense. Anyway, it seems Valve is working hard on SteamOS compatibility with the latest handheld releases —even if they're increasingly looking like some of the biggest victims of the RAMpocalypse so far.
